item.title: 6 Ways to Reset Your Busy Workday
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

6 Ways to Reset Your Busy Workday

Try these micro-resets to help you cope with a full day of meetings.

Posted August 21, 2026

Key points
  • Resets are small things you can do to break up your busy day and pause and refresh.
  • Research-supported strategies, such as breathing techniques and actions that help you reset.
  • Swap video calls for phone walks to increase creativity and gain restorative movement and sunlight.

This post was coauthored by Scott J. Allen, Ph.D. and Ron Riggio

Let’s face it, your workday is probably jammed full of Zoom and live meetings, back-to-back, with urgent email, texts, and phone calls in between. Your brain and nervous system never get the memo that they're allowed to reset.

This setup has costs. The version of you at 4:45pm, after seven straight meetings, is not the one who showed up sharp at 9am.

So, how do you stay centered, present, and clear-thinking throughout the day? Resets are the answer!

These resets are easy to use and don’t take a lot of time or resources. Try them out. What works for one person may not work for everyone, so experiment.

  1. Turn the Meeting Into a Walk-and-Talk. Sitting across a table puts people in a posture of evaluation, reading expressions and managing eye contact. Walking side-by-side removes that entirely, and conversations tend to open up. This works especially well for one-on-ones and brainstorming sessions where you want ideas to flow rather than get pinned down by formality. Apple’s Steve Jobs was famous for this and research supports its efficacy.
  2. Take a Quick, Effective, Physiological “Sigh.” Stanford neuroscientist Andrew Huberman and colleagues have popularized the technique (Balban, et al., 2023) of taking two inhales through the nose, back-to-back, followed by one long, slow exhale through the mouth. The double inhale reopens collapsed air sacs in your lungs, and the extended exhale activates your parasympathetic nervous system, the part responsible for calming you down. It takes about fifteen seconds and works anywhere. Here’s a brief video explaining the practice.
  3. Turn the Video Call into a Phone Call and Walk. If the agenda is a conversation rather than a shared document, ask to dial in instead of logging on. Cameras off, shoes on, and you get sunlight, movement, and a change of scenery, none of which a video call can provide. There’s also good evidence that walking increases creative output.
  4. Do a Random Act of Generosity. Cover someone’s coffee. Volunteer for the task nobody wants. Send team members a surprise note of gratitude. Research shows that giving activates the brain’s reward centers in ways similar to receiving. It’s a win-win.
  5. Try the Doorway Reset. Before you go into the next meeting or start the next conversation, pause for ten seconds at the threshold. Name one thing you want to bring into it, such as curiosity, patience, or full attention, and one thing you want to leave behind. Psychologists call this an event boundary, and studies show that consciously marking the transition between contexts helps your mind let go of the last one.
  6. Shrink Your Meetings. Try a 25-minute meeting instead of a 30-minute meeting. The reclaimed minutes make the difference between arriving at your next one already behind and arriving with a moment to reset. Use the gap on purpose: stand up, grab some water, look out the window. In any case, it’s a good strategy to set time limit defaults that make more sense.

None of these are complicated. What they require is a willingness to test something small and pay attention to what happens. Try one out this week. See if it changes how centered, grounded, present, and clear you feel by Friday.

item.title: Is Parenting Necessarily an Exercise in Exerting Power?
item.description:
Parenting

Is Parenting Necessarily an Exercise in Exerting Power?

Is a parental exercise of power necessarily a bad thing?

Posted August 21, 2026

Key points
  • Parental power can be used destructively.
  • But it can also be used for the good of the child.
  • Three options for dealing with misbehavior are punishment, consequences and collaborative consequence setting.

Recently, a colleague wrote to me about one of my most recent blog posts. In the post, I talked about the need for punishment and/or consequences when children or teens break a rule or behave in a way that the parents have told them not to. My colleague objected to my suggesting that punishment may be an option. He said, "I prefer consequences. Punishment for me evokes power."

And this raised a question for me: is the parent-child relationship one in which there is an inherently unequal power dynamic?

In Childism: Confronting Prejudice Against Children, psychoanalyst and political theorist Elisabeth Young-Bruehl argued that the parent-child relationship features a profound, inescapable asymmetry of power that leaves a lifelong psychological trace on the child. Rather than treating the natural dependency of a child as a neutral state, she wrote that adults weaponize this power imbalance through a deep-seated, systemic prejudice she called "childism."

She went on to say that childism emerges from three basic sources:

  1. The desire for absolute control: Some parents feel they own their child, which she felt can lead to harsh discipline and a wish to control the child and make them what the parent wants them to be, rather than who they are.
  2. Entitled superiority: This dynamic results from what Young-Bruel called the unexamined assumption that adults are automatically more rational, credible, and deserving of authority.
  3. Erasure of agency: This imbalance results in the adult tendency to dismiss or pathologize children's emotions and rights because of their age.

While I am not an authority on Young-Bruehl's work, it is nonetheless easy for me to see the importance of what she had to say.

The parent who does not reflect on their fantasy of who their unborn child will be, who is not able to separate out their own wish for who they want that child to be from who their child is as a person, and the parent who is unaware of their unconscious desires to "make" a child into a certain kind of person rather than allowing the child to emerge as who they are, is at risk for using discipline for the wrong reasons and toward an unhealthy end.

At the same time, we know that all children do need guidance, structure, consistent expectations, and, at times, discipline. Children are not born knowing how to contain and channel their impulses, and they often need help doing so.

Of course, we should not treat our children as extensions of ourselves or carriers of our own ambitions, but nor can we treat our children as complete equals at all times. There are moments — many moments — when raising children that we have to assert our authority as parents to keep them from harming themselves or others, and when we need to guide them toward gradually containing, channeling, and taking more responsibility for their own impulses and behavior.

So, how do we do this?

Do we embrace our power in those moments or do we reject it as inherently unjust? Do we exert our authority over our children or do we refrain?

To address Young-Bruehl's work, it is important to note that she makes a distinction between adults who are "childist" and those who are not. Those adults who believe that their own needs and wishes always come first over their child's are inherently childist. Those adults who feel it necessary to impose their own unmet needs and wishes onto their children, who insist that their children serve the needs of the parent to become who the parent wishes they had become or to become a replica of the parent, are misusing their power and authority.

But this is not the case with all parents, all power, and all authority.

In other words, authority and power in parenting, as in government and in life in general, can be used for good or ill. To eschew parental authority entirely would be to throw the proverbial baby out with the proverbial bathwater.

When a child or teen does something they have been asked not to do, the parent needs to find a way to deal with this. Whether they do so with harsh discipline or gentle parenting — or something in between — is a matter of choice, which can be determined by the relative severity of the infraction, the personality of the child, the personality of the parent, and the parent's parenting philosophy.

For example, a child who fools around over and over again just before bed may be given the consequence of having one less book read to them that night. Parents will find that even such minor consequences can elicit a big reaction in small children. They may cry and carry on for quite a while when given such a consequence. The child may feel that this is an unfair exercise of parental authority. But if a parent can hold firm and avoid the temptation to give in, the child can learn a valuable lesson — which is that they have parents who are trustworthy, able to set reasonable limits and, true to their word, will follow through on consequences that have been mentioned. The child learns that fooling around just before bed is not a good idea.

With more important infractions, for example, if a child hurts another family member on purpose, or if they do something which could be dangerous to themselves, this is the time when a more serious response from the parent is necessary. And in my opinion, it is the parent's job, not an exercise in the unfair use of power, for the parent to help their child by imposing a consequence that is meaningful — and which we might label as punishment. It is the parent's job to help their child to learn to stay safe and to treat others with decency, and in some cases, punishment for failing to do so may be the most impactful consequence.

Having parental power is an awesome responsibility. And, as Young-Bruehl made clear, parents must keep in mind that their use of their power may be a reflection of unconscious wishes. As such, parents are well advised to continually reflect on how they are disciplining their children and why — and to examine if perhaps they are acting on some less rational motivations rather than more consistently serving the well-being of their children.

And, interestingly, for those who want to share power with their children and teens, there is a possible third option beyond parentally imposed consequences and punishment — and that is called "collaborative consequence setting". Delany Rustin, a pediatrician, discussed this in a recent Screenagers blog post. She said that when an older child or teen misbehaves, the parent can try something new and ask the child what they think their consequence should be. She says that this increases the possibility that the child will actually think about why what they did was not OK. She also says that doing this supports children's maturation, and it can result in kids being less oppositional and more kind as people.

With collaborative consequence setting, kids have less of an opportunity to think that their consequence is unfair, since they have a part in setting the consequence; the parent becomes less of an authority and more of a collaborative partner, and both parent and child have an opportunity for dialogue rather than argument.
